items.readable_text:
Content:
The invertible matrix theorem tells us that if [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n \times n] matrix with full rank (i.e., [MATH: \mathrm{rank}(A)=n]), then there exists a unique inverse matrix [MATH: A^{-1}] such that

Content:
[MATH: AA^{-1}=A^{-1}\!A=I_n,]

Content:
where [MATH: I_n] denotes the [MATH: n \times n] identity matrix.

Content:
There are two questions that we can ask:

Content:
- Can we extend the notion of an inverse matrix to one that works for [MATH: n\times n] matrices [MATH: A] where [MATH: \mathrm{rank}(A) < n?]
- Is it possible to generalize the concept of an inverse to non-square matrices?

Content:
The answer to both questions is yes! This generalization of the inverse of [MATH: A] is called the pseudoinverse of [MATH: A,] and is denoted [MATH: A^+.] The dimensions of [MATH: A^+] are the same as [MATH: A^T.]

Content:
As an example, let's consider the [MATH: {\color{red}{3}}\times {\color{blue}{2}}] matrix [MATH: A] and its corresponding pseudoinverse, given below:

Content:
[MATH: [5|0; 0|1; 0|0]]

Content:
- Computing [MATH: A^{+}\!A,] we have
[MATH: A^{+}A|= (1)/(5)[1|0|0; 0|5|0] ⋅ [5|0; 0|1; 0|0]; = [1|0; 0|1]]
which is the identity matrix [MATH: I_{\color{blue}{2}}.]
- Computing [MATH: A\!A^{+},] we have
[MATH: AA^{+}|= [5|0; 0|1; 0|0] ⋅ (1)/(5)[1|0|0; 0|5|0]; = [1|0|0; 0|1|0; 0|0|0],]
which is almost the identity matrix [MATH: I_{\color{red}{3}}.]

Content:
We can explain this result using the following properties of the pseudoinverse:

Content:
- If the columns of an [MATH: m\times {\color{blue}{n}}] matrix [MATH: A] are linearly independent, then [MATH: A^+A = I_{\color{blue}{n}}.]
- If the rows of an [MATH: {\color{red}{m}}\times n] matrix [MATH: A] are linearly independent, then [MATH: AA^+ = I_{\color{red}{m}}.]

Content:
In the example above, the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly independent, but the rows are not.

Content:
Moreover, the notion of a pseudoinverse is consistent with inverse matrices. In particular,

Content:
> If [MATH: A] is an invertible square matrix, then [MATH: A^{+} = A^{-1}.]

Content:
This lesson will discuss how to compute the pseudoinverse for any matrix, starting with an important special case.

Content:
Consider the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [4|0; 3|0; 0|2]]

Content:
and its singular value decomposition [MATH: A=U \Sigma V ^T,] where

Content:
[MATH: [(4)/(5)|0|− (3)/(5); (3)/(5)|0|(4)/(5); 0|1|0]]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \Sigma] contains a row of zeros. In these situations, it's possible to simplify the decomposition of [MATH: A.] This simplified decomposition is called the reduced singular value decomposition of [MATH: A.]

Content:
First, we note that [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 3 \times 2] matrix. In addition, the matrix [MATH: \Sigma] has two non-zero singular values on its main diagonal, so the rank of [MATH: A] is [MATH: \color{blue}r=2.]

Content:
To find our reduced SVD, we proceed as follows:

Content:
- First, we remove all zero rows and columns from [MATH: \Sigma.] In our example, we should delete the [MATH: 3]rd row since it contains only zeros. Notice that we obtain a square invertible matrix of rank [MATH: {\color{blue}2}{:}]
[MATH: [5|0; 0|2; 0|0]]
- Next, we remove all extra columns of [MATH: U] starting from the right, keeping only [MATH: \color{blue}2] columns. In our example, we should delete the [MATH: 3]rd column:
[MATH: (4)/(5)|0|− (3)/(5); (3)/(5)|0|(4)/(5); 0|1|0]
- Finally, we remove all extra columns of [MATH: V] starting from the right, keeping only [MATH: \color{blue}2] columns. In our example, we should keep [MATH: V] as it is since it already has only [MATH: 2] columns:
[MATH: [1|0; 0|1]]

Content:
The reduced singular value decomposition of [MATH: A] is then given by

Content:
[MATH: A = U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T.]

Content:
So, in our example, we have

Content:
[MATH: [(4)/(5)|0; (3)/(5)|0; 0|1]]

Content:
In general, a singular value decomposition

Content:
[MATH: A=U \Sigma V^T]

Content:
of an [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A] is not unique. However, we can always simplify it to the corresponding reduced singular value decomposition

Content:
[MATH: A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T]

Content:
with the following properties:

Content:
- [MATH: \Sigma_r] is a square diagonal matrix of size [MATH: r\times r,] where [MATH: r\leq \min\{m,n\}] is the rank of [MATH: A.] The main diagonal of [MATH: \Sigma_r] contains the non-zero singular values [MATH: \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_r] of [MATH: A] in descending order.
- [MATH: U_r] is a [MATH: m\times r] matrix obtained by keeping only the first [MATH: r] columns of [MATH: U.]
- [MATH: V_r] is a [MATH: n \times r] matrix obtained by keeping only the first [MATH: r] columns of [MATH: V.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The invertible matrix theorem tells us that if [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n \times n] matrix with full rank (i.e., [MATH: \mathrm{rank}(A)=n]), then there exists a unique inverse matrix [MATH: A^{-1}] such that

Content:
[MATH: AA^{-1}=A^{-1}\!A=I_n,]

Content:
where [MATH: I_n] denotes the [MATH: n \times n] identity matrix.

Content:
There are two questions that we can ask:

Content:
- Can we extend the notion of an inverse matrix to one that works for [MATH: n\times n] matrices [MATH: A] where [MATH: \mathrm{rank}(A) < n?]
- Is it possible to generalize the concept of an inverse to non-square matrices?

Content:
The answer to both questions is yes! This generalization of the inverse of [MATH: A] is called the pseudoinverse of [MATH: A,] and is denoted [MATH: A^+.] The dimensions of [MATH: A^+] are the same as [MATH: A^T.]

Content:
As an example, let's consider the [MATH: {\color{red}{3}}\times {\color{blue}{2}}] matrix [MATH: A] and its corresponding pseudoinverse, given below:

Content:
[MATH: [5|0; 0|1; 0|0]]

Content:
- Computing [MATH: A^{+}\!A,] we have
[MATH: A^{+}A|= (1)/(5)[1|0|0; 0|5|0] ⋅ [5|0; 0|1; 0|0]; = [1|0; 0|1]]
which is the identity matrix [MATH: I_{\color{blue}{2}}.]
- Computing [MATH: A\!A^{+},] we have
[MATH: AA^{+}|= [5|0; 0|1; 0|0] ⋅ (1)/(5)[1|0|0; 0|5|0]; = [1|0|0; 0|1|0; 0|0|0],]
which is almost the identity matrix [MATH: I_{\color{red}{3}}.]

Content:
We can explain this result using the following properties of the pseudoinverse:

Content:
- If the columns of an [MATH: m\times {\color{blue}{n}}] matrix [MATH: A] are linearly independent, then [MATH: A^+A = I_{\color{blue}{n}}.]
- If the rows of an [MATH: {\color{red}{m}}\times n] matrix [MATH: A] are linearly independent, then [MATH: AA^+ = I_{\color{red}{m}}.]

Content:
In the example above, the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly independent, but the rows are not.

Content:
Moreover, the notion of a pseudoinverse is consistent with inverse matrices. In particular,

Content:
> If [MATH: A] is an invertible square matrix, then [MATH: A^{+} = A^{-1}.]

Content:
This lesson will discuss how to compute the pseudoinverse for any matrix, starting with an important special case.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Pseudoinverse of an Almost Diagonal Matrix

Content:
For an almost zero [MATH: {\color{red}{m}}\times {\color{blue}{n}}] matrix with non-zero entries

Content:
[MATH: \sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r]

Content:
on the main diagonal only, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the almost zero [MATH: {\color{blue}{n}}\times {\color{red}{m}}] matrix with non-zero entries

Content:
[MATH: {\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}]

Content:
on the main diagonal only.

Content:
For example, for the matrix [MATH: A,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [3|0|0; 0|4|0]]

Content:
we calculate its pseudoinverse as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A^{+}|= [3|0|0; 0|4|0]^{+}; = [3^{− 1}|0; 0|4^{− 1}; 0|0]; = (1)/(12)[4|0; 0|3; 0|0]]

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix

Example Prompt:
For the matrix
[MATH: [6|0; 0|4; 0|0]] find the pseudoinverse [MATH: A^+.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For an "almost" zero [MATH: m \times n] matrix with non-zero entries

[MATH: \sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r]

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero [MATH: n \times m] matrix with entries

[MATH: {\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}]

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: A^{+}|= [6|0; 0|4; 0|0]^{+}; = [6^{− 1}|0|0; 0|4^{− 1}|0]; = (1)/(12)[2|0|0; 0|3|0].]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Finding the Pseudoinverse Using Singular Value Decomposition

Content:
There are many ways to find the pseudoinverse of a given matrix [MATH: A.] One way is to use the singular value decomposition of [MATH: A{:}]

Content:

[MATH: A=U \Sigma V ^T]
is a singular value decomposition of [MATH: A,] then the pseudoinverse of [MATH: A] is given by
[MATH: A^+ = V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T,]
where [MATH: \Sigma^+] is the pseudoinverse of [MATH: \Sigma.]
